planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or stratify seed in a moist medium in the refrigerator for 8–10 weeks before spring sowing; yellowhorn strongly prefers excellent drainage and a drier continental-type climate, so it is best suited to zone 8 in drier margins of the Gulf region rather than humid, heavy-clay coastal ground.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, fast-draining, even poor or rocky soil; yellowhorn is a small deciduous tree native to northern China where it grows on dry hillsides, and it is notably drought tolerant once established but intolerant of wet feet or heavy, poorly drained clay. In spring it puts on a striking floral display of white, horse-chestnut-like flower panicles marked with red-to-yellow throats, followed in late summer by leathery green seed capsules that split open to release large, dark, chestnut-flavored seeds edible raw or roasted. Trees need several years of establishment before producing a meaningful nut crop, and while broadly self-fertile, planting more than one seedling improves pollination and yield. Give it a full-sun, well-drained site away from irrigation runoff or low spots where water collects.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree only where winters stay frost-free or nearly so; Sweetheart is self-fertile and bears reliably without a pollenizer tree, which makes it a more forgiving choice than Brewster for growers at the marginal, subtropical edge of lychee range.

directions: Sweetheart is a widely recommended Florida and Gulf Coast lychee cultivar prized because it is self-fertile and sets a reliable crop even in climates too marginal to trigger consistent flowering and fruit set in less adaptable cultivars such as Brewster. It bears clusters of medium-sized, bumpy-skinned red fruit with sweet, juicy, aromatic flesh and a comparatively small seed. Plant in full sun in deep, acidic, well-drained soil, sheltered from strong wind, and protect young trees from any frost since even brief freezes can kill unestablished plants. Lychee needs a brief, cool, relatively dry period in winter to initiate flower buds, so avoid heavy fertilizing or irrigation in late fall and winter; once flowering begins, water and feed generously through fruit development.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lychee Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
California Rare Fruit Growers — Lychee Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Subtropical Fruit for South Texas

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after frost danger passes; Lila is among the most cold-hardy avocado selections available, with mature wood reported to survive brief drops into the high teens °F, making it a realistic option for zone 8b–9 Gulf Coast gardens willing to give young trees frost protection in their first winters.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, fast-draining soil, since avocado roots are extremely sensitive to waterlogging and root rot. Lila is a Mexican-race selection bred specifically for cold hardiness, combining the anise-scented foliage and thin, smooth skin typical of that race with eating quality that many growers rate above other ultra-hardy Mexican-type avocados. As with most avocados, fruit set improves when a second tree of the complementary flowering type is planted nearby, though a single Lila can still produce fruit on its own. Water regularly during the growing season but let the soil dry between waterings, mulch well to protect the shallow root system, and shield young trees from hard freezes during their first two or three winters until the trunk and canopy have matured.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Avocado Fruit Facts
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Avocado Production in Texas
University of California Cooperative Extension — Cold-Hardy Avocado Varieties

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring; in zone 9 plant March–May. Pike is a cold-hardy, good-flavored white sapote selection often recommended as an alternative to Vernon for marginal, zone 9 Gulf Coast plantings, and it is self-fruitful so a single tree will set fruit without a pollinator.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil sheltered from strong wind; Pike is a California-selected white sapote cultivar valued for combining good cold tolerance with rich, high-quality fruit, making it a popular alternative where growers want more reliable cropping than some of the less flavorful ultra-hardy selections offer. The medium to large, thin-skinned fruit ripens from green to pale yellow-green and has smooth, custard-like flesh with a sweet flavor often described as a cross between banana and vanilla pudding. Trees grow quickly and can become large, so allow ample room and prune after harvest to keep the canopy manageable and encourage branching for the following year's crop. Pick fruit once it softens slightly at the stem end and finish ripening at room temperature for a few days before eating.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — White Sapote Fruit Facts
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White Sapote for Florida Landscapes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Subtropical Fruit Trees for South Texas
